title: Your Speech May Contain Hidden Information About How Fast You’re Aging - Nautilus
gist: A Science Advances paper led by neuroscientists at Chile's Adolfo Ibáñez University studied nearly 3,000 Spanish-speaking adults across five Latin American countries, finding that extralexical speech features such as pauses and tone may reveal how fast the brain is aging.

insights.claim: A new Science Advances paper suggests extralexical features of speech — pauses, tone, emphasis — may carry information about how fast the brain is aging.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Voice-based biomarkers could enable cheap, scalable cognitive screening — a target for digital health and AI diagnostics firms.
insights.quote: these extralexical features of speech may contain even more information about our aging brains
insights.locator: Speech contains a lot of information

insights.claim: How people speak, not the content of their words, may be the more informative signal about cognitive aging.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Suggests acoustic/prosodic AI models rather than language-content models for dementia screening.
insights.quote: What you say truly isn’t as important as how you say it
insights.locator: Your Speech May Contain Hidden Information

insights.claim: Researchers led by neuroscientists from Chile's Adolfo Ibáñez University recruited nearly 3,000 Spanish-speaking adults from Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Mexico and Peru.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: A large multi-country non-English cohort broadens validity of speech biomarkers beyond English-speaking populations.
insights.locator: Researchers led by a team of neuroscientists

insights.claim: The cohort included healthy adults as well as people with frontotemporal dementia, Alzheimer's disease and other forms of mild cognitive impairment.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Inclusion of multiple dementia types suggests potential for differential diagnosis tools.
insights.locator: Researchers led by a team of neuroscientists

insights.claim: If speech features track brain aging across healthy and impaired groups, speech analysis could become a non-invasive way to flag Alzheimer's and other cognitive impairment.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Watch for commercial voice-biomarker products and partnerships with Alzheimer's drug developers needing early-detection funnels.
insights.locator: Researchers led by a team of neuroscientists
